lead: React does not use HTML's onchange attribute. It gives you camelCase event props such as onClick and onChange, and each prop holds a JavaScript function. For forms, React goes further: the input's value is kept in state, and every keystroke updates that state. The browser shows what state says. This one-way flow gives a single source of truth for login forms, search boxes, checkout pages, and child components that must report a value upward.
prereq: You need Chapter 5.1 for JSX and Chapter 5.2 for state and the updater form.

sections.h3: Events are props that hold functions

blocks.text: JSX event props are camelCase: onClick, onChange, onSubmit. The value is a function, not a string. onClick={handleClick} passes the function, and React calls it on click. onClick={handleClick()} calls it during render and passes the result, usually undefined. That is the classic bug in the traps below.

React hands your handler a synthetic event object e. It wraps the browser event, so the same code works across browsers. e.target is the element that fired the event. e.target.value is an input's current text. e.target.name is its name attribute. e.preventDefault() stops the browser's default action, such as reloading the page when a form is submitted.
To pass an argument, wrap the call in an arrow: onClick={() => remove(id)}. The arrow is created during render; remove(id) runs only on click.

Events also carry data from child to parent. The parent passes a function prop, for example onChange={handleName}. The child calls props.onChange('R') when its value changes. The parent stores R in state and re-renders.

sections.h3: Controlled inputs: state holds the value

blocks.text: A controlled input takes its value from state and reports every change back to state: const [name, setName] = useState(''); and setName(e.target.value)} />. The user types R. onChange fires, setName('R') updates state, React re-renders, and the input receives value='R'. State, not the browser, holds the text. If you set value but forget onChange, the input is read-only: typing changes nothing and React warns in the console.

For many fields, keep one object and use the field's name: const [form, setForm] = useState({email: '', password: ''}); and const change = e => setForm({...form, [e.target.name]: e.target.value});. [e.target.name] is a computed property, so one handler updates email or password. The spread ...form copies the other field.

textarea uses value, not child text. select puts value on the select, not selected on each option. A checkbox uses checked={agree} with onChange={e => setAgree(e.target.checked)}. A radio group gives every radio the same name and uses checked={choice === 'male'}. A file input is always uncontrolled: read e.target.files.
For a small uncontrolled form, use useRef: const ref = useRef(); , then read ref.current.value on submit. Controlled inputs are preferred when you need live validation.

sections.h3: Child reports upward, and the form submits

blocks.text: Child-to-parent communication uses a callback prop. The parent owns state and passes a function: function PasswordField({value, onChange}) { return onChange(e.target.value)} />; }. The parent renders setForm({...form, password: v})} />. The child never edits the parent's state directly; it calls the function it was given. The parent updates state, and both parent and child re-render with the new value.

Submit handling goes on the form:
. In the handler call e.preventDefault() first. Without it the browser sends a GET request, the page reloads, and your state is lost. Then validate: if (password.length < 6) setError('Password too short'); else setError('');. Show {error &&

{error}

}. The check runs again on the server, because browser validation can be bypassed (see Unit 4, form processing).
Validation messages live in state, usually a separate string. Render them next to the field, and clear them when the user edits.

examples.question: A login form starts with state {email: '', password: ''}. The user types ravi@example.com into email, then pass123 into password, and clicks Submit. (a) What is the email string's length? (b) How many onChange calls does the password field make while typing pass123? (c) Does pass123 pass a length ≥ 6 check? (d) If the password were 123, what message appears? (e) What does preventDefault stop?
steps: Each keystroke fires one onChange. pass123 has 7 characters, so 7 calls.
length('pass123') = 7. 7 ≥ 6 is true, so validation passes and error stays ''.
length('123') = 3. 3 < 6 is true, so setError('Password too short') runs.
e.preventDefault() stops the browser's default submit, which would reload the page.
State after email typing is {email: 'ravi@example.com', password: ''}; after password typing it is {email: 'ravi@example.com', password: 'pass123'}.
examples.answer: The email is 16 characters; pass123 makes 7 onChange calls and passes the length ≥ 6 check; 123 gives 'Password too short'; preventDefault stops the page reload.
examples.check:
email = 'ravi@example.com'
pw = 'pass123'
short = '123'
print(len(email))
print(len(pw))
print(len(short))
print(6)

traps: onClick={handleClick()} runs during render, not on click. Use onClick={handleClick} or onClick={() => handleClick(id)}.
An input with value but no onChange is read-only, and React prints a warning in the console.
A checkbox uses e.target.checked, not e.target.value. Every radio in one group needs the same name attribute.
Forgetting e.preventDefault() in onSubmit reloads the page and wipes the state.
A file input cannot be controlled; setting value is ignored. Read e.target.files instead.

quiz.q: What is the difference between onClick={f} and onClick={f()}?
quiz.a: onClick={f} passes the function and React calls it on click. onClick={f()} calls f during render and passes its return value, usually undefined.

quiz.q: Why does <input value={name} /> without onChange stay read-only?
quiz.a: The value always comes from state. Typing changes the browser's display briefly, but no handler updates state, so React re-renders with the same value and the text does not stay.

quiz.q: State is form = {email: '', password: ''}. Write one onChange handler that updates either field using e.target.name.
quiz.a: const change = e => setForm({...form, [e.target.name]: e.target.value}); The spread copies the other field, and the computed property uses the input's name.

quiz.q: A child must send a selected id to its parent. Describe the callback prop flow and where state lives.
quiz.a: The parent owns the state and passes a function prop such as onSelect={id => setSelected(id)}. The child calls props.onSelect(id) on click. The parent state changes, and the parent re-renders.

quiz.q: Write the JSX for a checkbox whose state variable is agree and whose setter is setAgree.
Why call e.preventDefault() before validation in onSubmit?
quiz.a: Without it the browser performs the default form submission, usually a GET request that reloads the page and discards React state. preventDefault keeps the page and lets React validation run.

quiz.q: What are e.target.name and e.target.value used for?
quiz.a: e.target.name identifies which field fired the event. e.target.value is that field's current text.

quiz.q: When would you use useRef instead of a controlled input?
quiz.a: For a small form where you only need the value on submit and do not need live validation or re-rendering on each keystroke. Read ref.current.value in the submit handler.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production React forms often use libraries such as React Hook Form or Formik to avoid one state update per keystroke. React 19 adds form actions and useActionState, which connect a form to an async function. Accessibility work includes linking error text with aria-describedby. Search for controlled vs uncontrolled components, React Hook Form, and React form actions.
